title: Webb County Judge-elect Jerry Garza outlines priorities: jobs, rural roads, mental health care, town halls
excerpt: Jerry Garza, 66, takes office as Webb County judge on Jan. 1, 2027. He plans to push economic development, fix roads and drainage in rural areas and colonias, expand mental health and addiction treatment, and hold quarterly town halls in all four precincts.
content:
Webb County Judge-elect Jerry Garza, 66, says his first months in office will focus on bringing more business to the county, fixing roads and drainage in rural areas and colonias, expanding mental health and addiction treatment, and holding regular town hall meetings across all four precincts.

Garza, a former Webb County Precinct 4 commissioner who was born in Webb County and lives in Rio Bravo, takes office January 1, 2027, succeeding Tano Tijerina, who has served as county judge since 2015 and did not seek reelection, according to the Laredo Morning Times.

Garza won the Democratic primary on March 4, 2026, defeating Victor J. Ramirez by 24 votes, then faced no Republican opponent in the November 3 general election. He ran unsuccessfully for the same seat in 2022, and said his experience as a precinct commissioner prepared him for the role.

On economic development, Garza said he wants to grow and diversify the county's economy, make the county more competitive, attract businesses, make the economic development department more active, identify incentives for businesses, and strengthen workforce development and education partnerships to create jobs. He also wants to streamline the permitting process and reduce bureaucratic barriers.

On infrastructure, he said he wants to repair and modernize county roads, bridges, and water and drainage systems, with a focus on rural areas and colonias, and to address flooding concerns.

On public health, Garza said he wants to expand access to mental health services and substance-use treatment. Webb County has no state-operated psychiatric hospital, so people who need inpatient care must be transported elsewhere, a strain on families and law enforcement. He plans to work with state lawmakers and partners on sustainable solutions, consider county-led treatment options, and work with the Texas Health and Human Services Commission.

On community engagement, Garza said he plans to hold quarterly town hall meetings in all four precincts, make county government more transparent, accessible and responsive, and post agendas and materials online. "Residents should not have to wait until they have a problem to talk to their county judge," he said.

Garza said he will work with the current commissioners on the budget, take a close look at current spending and financial obligations and at the 2027 county budget, and work with Tijerina and the commissioners during the transition. Tijerina noted the county's $5 million in American Rescue Plan Act funds must be fully allocated by December 31, 2026. Garza said he does not plan to make changes to county staff.

Update — November 11, 2026

In a new interview with the Laredo Morning Times, Garza said his team is building a 100-day plan to shape how his four-year term begins. He formally takes office at midnight on January 1, and a public swearing-in will follow during the day the next week so more residents can attend. On roads, Garza said he has spoken with the Texas Department of Transportation, the city and other stakeholders about road needs. On the Bridge 4/5 project, he said he has not yet had a full briefing and knows it mainly from media coverage and Commissioners Court sessions; he called it a potential opportunity but urged caution about the kind of development it brings and whether roads could handle the added truck traffic. He also said he wants companies that already depend on the local crossings to open manufacturing or other operations in Webb County, naming health care and manufacturing as the sectors with the most room to grow.

Source: Laredo Morning Times (lmtonline.com), Valerie Gonzalez, Nov. 9, 2026.
